title: T. rex teeth indicate it ran as warm as an elephant
gist: UCLA researchers used clumped isotope thermometry on fossil T. rex teeth to measure a body temperature of about 36.3°C, similar to a modern elephant and well above the Cretaceous ambient climate, supporting the case that T. rex was a warm-blooded (endothermic) predator capable of ranging across most of the North American continent.

insights.claim: Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle's team measured T. rex body temperature using clumped isotope thermometry on tooth enamel, a technique that reads how often heavy carbon-13 and oxygen-18 isotopes bond together as the mineral forms, which depends on formation temperature regardless of the animal's body-water composition.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A methodological advance that removes a major confound (unknown ancient body-water composition) from prior oxygen-isotope dinosaur-temperature studies, making this result more reliable than earlier estimates.
insights.quote: Since tooth enamel forms inside a living body, the number of those clumped bonds records the animal’s body temperature, regardless of the water content in its body.

insights.claim: Earlier attempts to measure T. rex body temperature relied on oxygen isotope ratios in bones and teeth, a method confounded by the unknown composition of the animal's body water, a problem the new clumped-isotope method avoids.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Explains why prior body-temperature estimates for dinosaurs were considered unreliable, giving context for why this new result carries more weight than earlier work.
insights.quote: The problem was that those ratios depend not only on temperature but also on the composition of the water present in the animal’s body, which was something nobody could pin down for an extinct creature.

insights.claim: The team validated that the fossil enamel chemistry had not been altered over 66 million years underground by comparing enamel and dentin isotopic signatures, running infrared spectroscopy against modern alligator enamel, and checking that carbon isotopes matched the expected predator dietary signal.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Establishes the result's methodological rigor — the finding isn't just raw isotope data but has been cross-checked against multiple independent alteration tests.
insights.quote: It turned out the enamel and dentin of the same teeth had different isotopic signatures, which would be unlikely if their chemical composition had been changed after burial.
insights.locator: First, though, the team had to make sure

insights.claim: Three T. rex teeth from Montana's Hell Creek Formation yielded body temperatures of 37.3°C, 35.9°C, and 34.7°C, averaging 36.3°C ± 2.5°C — close to modern Indian and African elephants (~36°C) and within the range of large flightless birds like ostriches and emus.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The headline quantitative result: a specific, cross-checked body-temperature figure for T. rex that can now anchor future dinosaur-physiology comparisons.
insights.quote: Averaged together, T. rex had a body temperature of 36.3°, give or take 2.5°.

insights.claim: Crocodilians sampled from the same Hell Creek ecosystem averaged a body temperature of 30.9°C, consistent with modern crocodilian thermoregulation by basking, showing a clear gap between T. rex and cold-blooded reptiles of the same environment.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The crocodilian control group is what makes the T. rex result meaningful — the ~5.4°C gap mirrors the gap seen today between large mammals and crocodilians, strengthening the endothermy case.
insights.quote: The crocodilians the team used as a comparison came in at an average of 30.9°—in line with the preferred range of modern crocodilians

insights.claim: Contemporary environmental data (fossil freshwater mussels averaging 26°C, and climate models peaking at ~33°C in summer with 21°C mean annual temperature even under a hot scenario) show T. rex was consistently warmer than the Cretaceous world it inhabited.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Rules out the possibility that T. rex's elevated temperature was simply passive absorption of a hot ambient climate — it was actively warmer than its environment.
insights.quote: So T. rex was consistently warmer than the world it lived in.

insights.claim: The juvenile T. rex's measured temperature exceeded what body-size scaling models predict for a purely cold-blooded animal of its weight, leading the authors to argue — while acknowledging the debate isn't settled — that T. rex was likely a homeothermic endotherm generating its own metabolic heat, rather than relying solely on gigantothermy (large-body heat retention).
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Pushes back against the pure-gigantothermy explanation and toward active endothermy, a meaningfully different physiological picture with implications for T. rex's metabolic energy needs and predation strategy.
insights.quote: the team behind the new work argues that its results add to a growing body of evidence that T. rex was a homeothermic endotherm, an animal that kept a steady body temperature using its own metabolic heat, while acknowledging that the question is not yet settled

insights.claim: Using thermal tolerance data from 465 living mammals and birds combined with the measured T. rex temperature range and Cretaceous climate simulations, the researchers modeled that T. rex could have lived almost anywhere across the North American continent, including cold, high-latitude zones consistent with tyrannosaurid fossil finds in Alaska.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A concrete habitat-suitability prediction that extends beyond the known fossil record, suggesting T. rex's ecological range was far broader than where fossils have actually been found.
insights.quote: The conclusion was that T. rex could live almost anywhere on the continent.

insights.claim: The study's authors caution that with only three teeth sampled and small enamel portions analyzed to avoid fossil damage, the results could reflect a single growth season rather than year-round average body temperature, so a seasonal sampling bias cannot be fully ruled out.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: An explicit limitation the authors themselves flag — a reason to treat the 36.3°C figure as a solid but not fully conclusive estimate pending larger sample sizes.
insights.quote: the researchers acknowledge that with three teeth, they cannot fully rule out a seasonal bias
